title: Cash on the financial statements
subtitle: Cash & equivalents - the safest slice of assets
openingQuestion: What do cash and cash equivalents include?
openingOptions: Only the paper cash that happens to be sitting in the office till at this very moment
Cash, short-term bank deposits, and assets convertible to cash within 3 months
explanation: Cash and equivalents include cash on hand, bank deposits, and investments with an original term of three months or less - the criterion is converting to cash almost instantly without significant value fluctuation. This is the first line on the balance sheet and also the most trustworthy, since it's hard to distort with accounting estimates. But a lot of cash isn't automatically good: idle cash is capital that isn't earning a return.

realWorldExample.description: Apple maintains hundreds of billions of dollars in cash and short-term investments - partly for flexibility in M&A and buybacks, and partly criticised by investors as "idle capital" not being used efficiently.

quiz.question: Cash includes:
options: Cash and accounts receivable from customers
Cash plus all current assets
Cash + deposits + short-term certificates
Cash on hand and inventory
quiz.explanation: Receivables and inventory are current assets but not cash - each still has to be collected or sold, sometimes at a loss. Cash equivalents qualify only because they convert almost instantly with negligible price risk.

quiz.question: Cash is listed first because:
options: It has the largest value among assets
By alphabetical order of the line items
It has the lowest risk of losing value in the portfolio
It's the most liquid, usable right away
quiz.explanation: Balance sheet assets are ordered by liquidity, not by size, alphabet or safety. A large building sits below a small cash balance for exactly this reason: it cannot be spent tomorrow.

quiz.question: Low cash affects the ability to:
options: Pay off current liabilities on time
Issue additional shares to the market
Recognise revenue for that period
Compute depreciation on fixed assets
quiz.explanation: Issuing shares, recognising revenue and computing depreciation all proceed regardless of the bank balance - the first two are financing and accrual events, the third a non-cash allocation. Only settling obligations needs actual cash.

quiz.question: Cash equivalents must:
options: Convert to cash in under 12 months
Convert to cash in under 3 months
Be guaranteed for payment by a bank
Have a higher yield than deposit interest
quiz.explanation: Twelve months is the current-asset test, not the cash-equivalent one, which is far stricter. A bank guarantee does not shorten the maturity, and a yield above deposit rates signals exactly the price risk that disqualifies an instrument.

quiz.question: Buying a 10-year bond is recorded as:
options: A current asset
A long-term financing cost
A long-term investment
A cash equivalent
quiz.explanation: A ten-year maturity fails both the three-month cash-equivalent test and the one-year current-asset test. Nor is it a cost: buying a bond exchanges one asset for another, leaving the income statement untouched.

quiz.question: Is rising cash always good?
options: Not certain - it depends on the scale of revenue and the industry
Always bad because cash generates no profit
Always good because cash is a safe asset
Not certain - it depends on where the cash comes from
quiz.explanation: Cash from operations and cash from new borrowing look identical on the balance sheet but say opposite things about the business. Neither blanket answer holds: the source, not the level, is what the reader has to check.

quiz.question: A company shouldn't hold too much cash because:
options: Cash earns no return, so it should be put into further investment
Too much cash lowers the company's Current Ratio
Too much idle cash makes shareholders demand all of it be paid out as dividends
Too much cash raises the income tax owed
quiz.explanation: Holding cash raises the Current Ratio rather than lowering it, and it creates no taxable event - tax follows profit, not balances. Shareholders may ask for a payout, but they cannot compel the whole balance to be distributed.

keyTakeaways: Cash = the most liquid, lowest-risk asset
Cash position reflects both short-term health and long-term strategy

practicePrompt.question: Company A has 500 billion in cash from years of accumulated operating profit; company B also has 500 billion in cash but just got it by borrowing from a bank. Why should investors judge these two '500-billion cash' figures differently?
options: They shouldn't be judged differently, since cash is cash - its origin doesn't matter to a company's financial health
They should be judged differently: cash earned from operations is not the same as cash from borrowing
Company B should be rated higher for successfully raising additional external capital
Both companies should be rated poorly for holding too much cash that isn't earning a return
practicePrompt.explanation: Cash is the most liquid, lowest-risk asset on the balance sheet - but the origin of the cash matters: cash from operating profit is a good signal, cash from borrowed money comes with an interest obligation and higher risk, even when the current cash balance is identical.

summary.keyIdea: Cash = the most liquid, lowest-risk asset
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Add up your own highly liquid assets
application.message: Open every bank account and e-wallet you have, and add up the total cash and deposits with a term under 3 months - this is your real 'cash & equivalents'.
application.secondary: Compare this figure against one month of living costs to know whether you have enough of a safety buffer.

sections.text: Cash & Cash Equivalents always sits at the top of the current-assets list on the balance sheet - because it's the most liquid asset, usable immediately to pay debt, buy goods, or settle any obligation.

Pure cash includes paper currency and demand deposits at a bank. Cash equivalents are investments with liquidity nearly equal to cash - an original maturity of 3 months or less from the purchase date, for example short-term treasury bills, short-term certificates of deposit, or money market funds. Because their maturity is so short, the risk of value fluctuation is nearly zero.
Why a large cash balance is both a strength and a criticism

A company holding a lot of cash has a good buffer against economic volatility, ample resources for acquisitions (M&A), share buybacks when the price is attractive, or accelerated R&D investment when the opportunity arises. But long-term investors often ask the opposite question: cash sitting idle earns a savings-deposit rate far below the return shareholders expect the company to generate - if management has no clear plan for using it, that's wasted capital that should be returned to shareholders through dividends or buybacks.

items: A lot of cash + a clear investment/M&A plan: a positive signal, preparing for growth
A lot of cash + no plan to use it: shareholders may pressure for dividends or buybacks
Little cash + high debt: liquidity risk that needs close monitoring

sections.label: Restricted cash
sections.text: Part of a company's cash may be restricted from free use - for example, a bank guarantee deposit or a contract deposit. This amount, though sitting within 'cash' in the report, isn't freely usable - read the notes to the financial statements to identify it.
